I am immensely proud to be the Headteacher of Aureus School. I have a passion for comprehensive education and I firmly believe that every student deserves the opportunity to succeed. My approach is driven by my belief in inclusive education and centred around high expectations of all students.
As the only co-educational comprehensive school in Didcot we have a fantastic student body whose range of attributes contribute to making Aureus School a vibrant community. I have the privilege to be working with a talented, dedicated and enthusiastic staff body who are passionate about inspiring our young people every single day, enabling them to thrive.
Kirsty Rogers, Headteacher, Aureus School

Art
In Year 7, students will explore the formal elements of Art through a variety of creative activities, developing and refining their drawing, painting, printmaking, and 3D skills. Each formal element—line, tone, shape, form, texture, and colour—will be introduced and revisited throughout the year. Drawing will feature in every project as a core skill that supports and enhances all other aspects of the course. Students will also be encouraged to question and discuss the work of different artists, using these influences as inspiration for their own personal studies.
Year 7 Curriculum Overview - Art
In Year 8 Art, students will build on their knowledge and understanding of the formal elements through themes that encourage a more personal and creative response. They will refine their ability to critically analyse and evaluate both their own work and the work of others. Students will continue to develop their drawing, painting, 3D (clay) and printmaking skills, while experimentation with a range of media will allow them to explore a broad variety of creative techniques.
Year 8 Curriculum Overview - Art
Students will continue their journey toward becoming confident and independent artists in Year 9. They will refine their skills in painting, drawing, and printmaking, developing greater control and confidence as young artists. Throughout the year, they will explore a variety of artists to respond to, gaining valuable contextual knowledge that will deepen their understanding of artistic practice and inform their own creative work.
Year 9 Curriculum Overview - Art
Students will continue with their journey to becoming confident and independent artists in year 10. This year will aim to continue to develop students' understanding of the 4 Assessment objectives, develop and begin to refine artistic skills and knowledge, building on their already growing Personal portfolio (worth 60%) whilst creating more fabulous work they are proud of. Throughout the year there will be points where we will begin to experience extended working times in preparation for the externally set assignment in year 11. Students will continue to keep a portfolio of their work that they will add to and refine throughout the 3 years. The art studio will be made available, where possible, to students during club time to enable them to extend and develop their learning further.

Geography
Geography Curriculum Map
In Geography during Term 1 & 2 Year 7 students improve their geographical skills, and discover the physical and human landscape of the UK. During Term 3 & 4 Year 7 explore water, rivers and flooding, and discover the human and physical Geography of Europe. Throughout Term 5 & 6 Year 8 investigate the different ecosystems around the globe and learn how to improve their fieldwork and research skills. Year 7 will study case studies, outlining key events in the Earth’s history, they will address the interaction between the physical and human world and how this can sometimes lead to conflict, while developing skills in interpreting geographical data, in map reading and in identifying and explaining geographical patterns and processes. Through this they will gain a deeper understanding of human and physical Geography, and the impact we have on the world around us
Year 7 Curriculum Overview - Geography
During term 1 & 2 Year 8 students discover the human and physical Geography of Asia, and how plate tectonics influence volcanoes and earthquakes. During Term 3 & 4 Year 8 learn how globalisation has impacted the world around us, and explore the world of Small Island Developing States (SIDS). Throughout Term 5 & 6 Year 8 investigate the different weather experienced across the UK and develop their understanding of sustainability locally and globally. Year 8 will study case studies, outlining key events in the Earth’s history, they will address the interaction between the physical and human world and how this can sometimes lead to conflict, while developing skills in interpreting geographical data, in map reading and in identifying and explaining geographical patterns and processes. Through this they will gain a deeper understanding of human and physical Geography, and the impact we have on the world around us.
Year 8 Curriculum Overview - Geography
During Term 1 & 2 Year 9 students discover the human and physical Geography of Africa, and how the world around us is impacted by looking at climate change, resource scarcity and the effects of both. During Term 3 & 4 Year 9 discover the physical and human Geography of South America, and explore the world of cold environments. Throughout Term 5 & 6 Year 9 investigate the landscapes and their physical processes, learning about coasts and rivers. Year 9 will study case studies, outlining key events in the Earth’s history, they will address the interaction between the physical and human world and how this can sometimes lead to conflict, while developing skills in interpreting geographical data, in map reading and in identifying and explaining geographical patterns and processes. Through this they will gain a deeper understanding of human and physical Geography, and the impact we have on the world around us.
Year 9 Curriculum Overview - Geography
Year 10 GCSE The Eduqas GCSE Geography A course progresses students from the extensive Key Stage 3 programme of study at Aureus School by deepening student’s knowledge and understanding of the world around them. The course builds onto the end of Year 9 with a broader study of landform processes and change in the UK. There is a focus upon river flooding which is a frequent hazard and students will gain an insight into how we manage flooding now and what can be done in the future. In November of the course students study the links between rural and urban areas and the reasons why more people live in cities than rural areas. Within this, students study the rural/urban links in countries at different levels of development, compared to the UK. In the Spring term students study tectonic processes and associated landforms and the vulnerability of communities in low income countries and how governments can mitigate impacts of tectonic hazards. In the summer term, students undertake the fieldwork component of the course in June, this is an opportunity to put into practise what students are learning in the classroom.
Year 10 Curriculum Overview - Geography
Year 11 students will continue their GCSEs during Autumn Term 1 by studying Weather, Climate and Ecosystems, using case studies to investigate patterns across the world. In Autumn Term 2 they will begin Social Development, using prior knowledge built from the past two years to learn how development is measured, and explore contemporary development issues. In Spring Term 1 & 2 we will begin to refine our practical fieldwork skills, allowing Year 11 students to further develop their skills in interpreting geographical data, in map reading and in identifying and explaining geographical patterns and processes. In Summer Term 1 & 2 we will complete exam preparations.

History
History Curriculum Map
History is taught for three hours a fortnight from the start of the year. Students will have the opportunity to learn core skills vital to this discipline such as chronological organisation, evidence analysis and evaluation of causation. Students in Year 7 will assess the organisation of society and the control exerted by monarchs both in the British Isles and abroad during the medieval period. Topics include the Norman conquest, King John and the Crusades. Selecting this time-period allows students to review how society is structured with personal rule increasingly supplemented by sophisticated bureaucracies.
Year 7 Curriculum Overview - History
In Year 8 students will build on the skills of inference, analysis and evaluation learned in their first year of secondary education to look at the changing relationship between England and the rest of the world. They will focus on the 16th to the 19th centuries, focusing on topics such as the English Civil Wars, the Renaissance and the Industrial Revolution.
Year 8 Curriculum Overview - History
In Year 9 students will build on the skills of inference, analysis and evaluation learned across the first two years of secondary History. Throughout the course we will make links to modern events such as the First World War, the Second World War, the Holocaust and the Post War World setting them in context to enable students to better understand some of the reasons behind modern international relations and conflicts.
Year 9 Curriculum Overview - History
Key Stage 4 History will build upon the fundamental historical concepts taught at KS3 such as change and continuity, significance , interpretations and source analysis. Our chosen exam board is Edexcel. The course is split into three papers which allows a wide breadth of historical knowledge to be obtained. Paper 1 is Medicine in Britain c1250-present and also includes a study of the Western Front in WW1. Paper 2 is made up of 2 sections: Early Elizabethan England 1558-88, and Superpower Relations and the Cold War, 1941-91. Paper 3 is a study of Weimar and Nazi Germany. Through these courses students gain a wide range of knowledge in British, European and World History. Year 10 Curriculum Overview - History
In Year 11, students will resume their GCSE studies - beginning by continuing their study of Weimar and Nazi Germany . Students will then move on to acquiring further skills to consolidate their knowledge of our GCSE topics in order to prepare them for our external examinations.

Subjects
Design Technology
Design Technology: Learning Journey
Food Technology In Year 7 Food Technology, pupils learn the basics of working safely in a kitchen. They are taught about food hygiene, cross-contamination and food poisoning, and how to reduce risks when preparing food. Pupils develop essential knife skills, including the bridge and claw techniques, and apply these skills when making simple, healthy dishes. Lessons also focus on teamwork, communication and organisation, with pupils working in pairs during practical activities. The curriculum introduces the Eatwell Guide, helping pupils understand healthy eating and balanced diets. By the end of Year 7, pupils will have gained confidence, practical skills and a strong foundation for future Food Technology learning.
Textiles Students will develop foundational hand-sewing skills, including the use of a running stitch and the ability to sew on a button. These practical skills support independence and have clear applications in everyday life. Students will then complete a practical assessment to demonstrate their competence, working towards differentiated success criteria. Building on these skills, students will explore fashion trends across different decades, analysing the social, cultural, and historical influences that shaped them. Students will apply this knowledge by designing outfits inspired by the styles of each era.
Product Design Students will be introduced to the workshop environment, many have little or no experience using workshop equipment and resistant materials such as wood metals and plastics. Students are required to understand procedures for working effectively and safely including basic Health and Safety procedures. Students will develop teamwork skills and confidence throughout the year. Coursework is set for the year to design and make a finished product. This will challenge students to think creatively and systematically, overcoming a variety of obstacles along the way to obtain a high-quality finished outcome. They will acquire and develop new skills in planning, drawing and problem solving. Students will develop the required skills to reflect on their own learning and the learning of others using strategies to respond to feedback effectively.
In addition to this, students will have the opportunity to take part in lunchtime DT clubs where they can advance their skills and explore more systems, techniques and equipment to extend their knowledge and explore their own interests around the subject.
Year 7 Curriculum Overview - DT
Year 8 Curriculum Overview: Food In Year 8 Food Technology, pupils build on their knowledge of healthy eating by developing a deeper understanding of the Eatwell Guide and macronutrients, including carbohydrates, protein and fats. Pupils explore where food comes from, learning about food that is grown, reared, caught and processed, and consider the environmental impact of food choices. The curriculum also focuses on food waste, encouraging pupils to think about sustainability and practical ways to reduce waste. Practical lessons continue to develop safe working practices, knife skills and hygiene, while introducing more complex recipes. Pupils work in pairs to strengthen their communication, organisation and teamwork skills, preparing them for greater independence in food preparation. By the end of Year 8, pupils will have increased confidence in the kitchen and a stronger understanding of nutrition, sustainability and food preparation.
Year 8 Curriculum Overview: Textiles Students will build on their prior learning from Year 7 by developing the skills required to safely set up and operate a sewing machine. They will learn key construction techniques, including sewing plain seams and hemming. Students will then complete a practical assessment to demonstrate their technical competence. Following this, they will study a range of fashion designers, exploring their backgrounds and sources of inspiration. Students will apply this knowledge by designing original garments influenced by the work and creative approaches of these designers.
Year 8 Curriculum Overview: Product Design In year 8, students will continue to develop skills and extend their knowledge of materials and processes. Students should begin to understand fundamental principles of health and safety in the workshop as well as teamworking skills. Students will develop confidence in the use of machines as well as problem solving and building resilience. This year students will be studying additional processes and materials. They will need to think creatively and analytically in order to produce a successful outcome. Students will develop the required skills to reflect on their own learning and the learning of others using strategies to respond to feedback effectively. In addition to this, students will have the opportunity to take part in lunchtime DT clubs where they can advance their skills and explore more systems, techniques and equipment to extend their knowledge and explore their own interests around the subject. This will allow students to make an informed decision at the end of KS3 regarding their GCSE options.
Year 8 Curriculum Overview - DT
Year 9 Year 9 Curriculum Overview: Food In Year 9 Food Technology, pupils explore international cuisine, learning how food reflects culture, tradition and global influences. Pupils study the characteristics of British food and examine how immigration has shaped the food we eat in the UK today. Practical lessons focus on cooking recipes from around the world, exposing pupils to a wide range of cuisines, ingredients and flavours. Through this, pupils continue to develop safe working practices, hygiene and knife skills, while gaining greater confidence and independence in the kitchen. Pupils also complete a small research project, developing skills in investigation, organisation and presentation. This prepares them for future GCSE study and helps build a deeper understanding of food, culture and society.
Year 9 Curriculum Overview: Textiles Students will consolidate and apply the skills and knowledge developed across Years 7 and 8 to collaboratively design and construct a garment using upcycled materials. This project is designed to deepen students’ understanding of sustainability and responsible design within a real-world context. Through structured collaborative working, students will develop essential personal and social skills, including teamwork, communication, and problem-solving. They will draw on their own creative influences to produce purposeful design solutions in response to a set brief, supporting the development of resilience, independence, and students’ spiritual, moral, social, and cultural understanding.
Year 9 Curriculum Overview: Product Design In year 9, students will begin the coursework for the Product Design GCSE through fun but challenging making projects. As in year 7 & 8 the design theory lessons are interwoven with practical tasks that put the learning into practice. In year 9, students are taught more advanced processes and an extended range of materials, building knowledge that is covered in year 10. Students will continue develop their confidence, safe working practices and teamwork throughout the year. This year students will be challenged with a mini design and making project of their own. Pupils will be asked to identify a problem area and produce a solution in the form of a finished made product to solve it. They will need to think creatively and analytically whilst displaying resilience and determination. Students will develop the required skills to reflect on their own outcomes and that of others using strategies to analyse and respond to feedback effectively.
Year 10 Catering and Hospitality Year 10 Curriculum Overview: Catering and Hospitality In Year 10, pupils begin the WJEC Level 1/2 Award in Hospitality and Catering, which is assessed through two components: Unit 1: The Hospitality and Catering Industry (40%) – a written examination
Unit 2: Hospitality and Catering in Action (60%) – non-examined assessment (coursework and practical work)
During Year 10, pupils focus primarily on Unit 1, developing a strong understanding of the hospitality and catering industry. They explore different hospitality and catering providers, job roles and career pathways, and the operation of front and back of house. Pupils also learn how businesses meet customer requirements and expectations. A significant part of the course is dedicated to health, safety and food hygiene, including HACCP, food safety legislation, allergies and intolerances, cross contamination, and the role of the Environmental Health Officer (EHO). This knowledge prepares pupils for both the written examination and real-world professional practice. Alongside theory, pupils are introduced to the NEA through a mock practical assessment, allowing them to understand the demands of the coursework component. In practical lessons, pupils practise a range of medium to complex cooking skills, focusing on organisation, time management, hygiene and presentation. This structured approach ensures pupils are well prepared for the final practical exam in Year 11. Y10 DT GCSE Students will embark on the theory of Product Design. This will include aspects of global trade, manufacturing and transportation, the environmental impact of manufacture, global issues relating to consumerism. We will also learn how to research, analyse and innovate, we will design solutions to real problems and learn about the latest techniques, processes and materials available to solve problems impacting all of us. Year 10 will set the students up with the knowledge and experience for year 11, when they will be expected to put all of this into practice. Pupils will be examined on their theory knowledge at the end of year 11 in a written paper forming 50% of their marks.
Year 11 Catering and Hospitality In Year 11, pupils complete the WJEC Level 1/2 Award in Hospitality and Catering, focusing on both the Non-Examined Assessment (NEA) and preparation for the final written examination. The year begins with pupils completing their official NEA practical assessment, which contributes 60% of the final grade. Pupils plan, prepare, cook and evaluate dishes in response to a set brief, demonstrating their understanding of nutrition, customer needs, organisation, time management, hygiene and presentation. This assessment allows pupils to apply the practical skills and industry knowledge developed throughout the course. Following the completion of the NEA, teaching focuses on revision for Unit 1, the written examination worth 40% of the final grade, which takes place in June. Pupils revisit key topics including hospitality and catering providers, front and back of house operations, customer requirements, health and safety, food safety, HACCP, allergens, cross contamination and the role of the Environmental Health Officer (EHO). Structured revision, exam practice and targeted support ensure pupils are confident, well prepared and able to achieve their best possible outcomes.
Students in year 11 will have been given their challenge at the end of year 10, they will be embarking on their main GCSE project. To design and make a solution to a problem they have identified. This is their Non-Examined Assessment (NEA) it is a single project spread over the entire year and forms 50% of their marks.

Global Citizenship
What does it mean to be a true global citizen?
At Aureus we want our students know the answer to this question. We are passionate about developing the whole child and providing them with knowledge, skills and understanding that will prepare them to play a full and active part in the world around them.
We cover a range of areas such as: Active Citizen, The Wider World/Careers, Life in Modern Great Britain, Health and Wellbeing, Political Participation and Relationships.

English Curriculum Map
What does the English Curriculum at Aureus strive to achieve?
The intent of our English curriculum is to secure fluency in the foundational processes of reading and writing. As these processes become increasingly automatic, pupils are able to devote greater cognitive attention to the central work of the subject: interpreting and crafting texts as representations of meaningful human experience. We believe that where pupils struggle to reach this level, the cause lies not in something inherent in the pupil, but in gaps in the earlier building blocks that make this level of thinking possible - gaps we can address through effective teaching.
How do students study English at Aureus?
Students study English through a structured approach to reading and writing. In reading, we prioritise securing fluency and checking understanding before asking pupils to interpret texts. In writing, we focus first on students’ ability to transcribe accurately and to manipulate sentence structures in a range of ways, enabling them to produce increasingly complex compositions of their own. At Key Stage 3, pupils study a broad range of texts and forms. Across Years 7–9, these texts are organised around four recurring literary themes: power, change, choice and identity. Encountering these themes in different texts and contexts allows pupils to see connections between ideas and to understand how writers represent similar experiences in different ways. Across all areas of study, we work to secure fluent reading and writing as the foundation for deeper thinking, so that all pupils are able to engage with and respond to the texts they study with increasing confidence and control. At Key Stage 4, pupils build on this foundation to meet the demands of GCSE study. In Year 10, they study the texts required for their English Literature GCSE, while continuing to develop the reading and writing fluency needed to interpret texts with precision and express ideas clearly in writing. Towards the end of the year, they prepare for their first set of mock examinations and complete the Spoken Language Endorsement. In Year 11, this focus sharpens into preparation for examinations in both English Language and Literature. Teaching is structured to consolidate pupils’ knowledge and refine their ability to read, interpret and write with control, so that they can demonstrate what they know in exam conditions and secure outcomes that give them the widest possible choice in their next steps beyond Aureus.
Why is studying English important?
The study of English is important because it gives pupils greater agency in a world where the ability to read, write and think clearly matters. By becoming fluent readers and writers, pupils gain access to the ideas, experiences and perspectives represented in texts, and develop the ability to understand and evaluate them. The ability to engage with and respond to meaning in texts - both now and in the future, and with the freedom for that choice to change over time - is something we believe no pupil should leave school without.

Computing Curriculum Map
Computing at Key Stage 3 (Years 7–9) Computing at Key Stage 3 builds students' confidence and capability as creators and users of technology. Across the three years they develop computational thinking, programming, and digital skills through practical, engaging work — and learn how the digital systems around them actually work. Year 7 In Year 7, students build strong foundations in computing — developing their digital literacy, computational thinking, and understanding of how computers and the digital world work. They learn to stay safe and responsible online, manage files, protect personal information and communicate well digitally, with skills taught through practical tasks rather than in isolation. They develop computational thinking by breaking problems down, spotting patterns and reasoning logically, take part in the national Bebras Challenge, and use spreadsheets as part of a growing digital toolkit. Students explore how computers work — the components inside a machine, how they connect as a system, and how information is stored and processed. They learn to program through block-based coding, then apply their skills hands-on with the BBC micro:bit, writing real code to control a physical device. They also develop creative and design skills through 3D modelling in Tinkercad. Lessons combine practical work, discussion and hands-on activities, building skills that support students across the curriculum and prepare them for Year 8.
Year 7 Curriculum Overview
Year 8 In Year 8, students build on their Year 7 foundations and go deeper — becoming more technical, more independent, and more creative in how they apply their computing skills. They deepen their understanding of how computers represent data — how numbers, text, images and sound are encoded in binary — and explore the Boolean logic that underpins how computers make decisions. They also take part in the national Bebras Challenge, applying computational thinking to a range of logic and problem-solving tasks. Programming takes a significant step forward. Students move from block-based coding into writing real text-based Python, then apply those skills to physical computing — programming the BBC micro:bit using MicroPython to build a project with sensors and inputs. Students investigate online reliability, learning to evaluate sources, spot misinformation and bias, and think critically about AI-generated content. They extend their spreadsheet and data-handling skills with more complex formulas and charts, and develop creative design skills through 3D modelling in SketchUp — designing spaces and objects with greater ambition than in Year 7. Lessons combine practical activities, discussion and independent problem-solving, preparing students for the demands of Year 9.
Year 8 Curriculum Overview
Year 9 In Year 9, students apply their computing skills across a range of ambitious, real-world contexts — a strong final year for every student that also builds firm foundations for those choosing GCSE Computer Science. They explore cyber security in depth — how systems are attacked, the laws that protect data and people (Computer Misuse Act, GDPR), and the role of social engineering and malware. They also study how computer systems work at a technical level: the CPU, fetch-execute cycle, memory and processing — content that connects directly to GCSE. Programming takes on new dimensions. Students take part in the national Bebras Challenge, apply their Python skills to physical computing with the BBC micro:bit, and later use MakeCode Arcade to design and build their own game — combining programming logic, creative design and iterative problem-solving. They develop data and digital skills through the Digital Toolkit strand, using spreadsheets to model scenarios and interpret results. They also work with Fusion 360, professional-grade CAD software, to design and engineer 3D objects to a brief — a significant step up from earlier years. Lessons combine practical work, discussion and independent problem-solving. Computing is more than programming: students learn how systems work and apply a range of techniques to solve problems — valuable thinking and creative skills highly relevant beyond school and in the modern workplace.
Computer Science at KS4 At Key Stage 4, students study GCSE Computer Science, following the OCR GCSE Computer Science (J277) course. Computer Science is a creative and challenging subject that develops students' ability to think logically, solve problems and design digital solutions. Building on the foundations from Key Stage 3, students deepen their understanding of how computer systems work and how programs are created. The course is structured around two papers: Computer Systems and Computational Thinking, Algorithms and Programming. In the first, students explore how hardware, memory, networks, security and software work together, and how data is represented at a technical level. In the second, they develop their programming skills in Python — designing algorithms, writing and testing programs, and solving increasingly complex problems. Throughout the course, students learn to design, write, test and refine programs, and consider the wider impact of technology on individuals and society. They develop resilience, precision and confidence through practical work and applied problem-solving. By the end of the course, students have a strong understanding of how digital systems operate and the skills to progress to further study in computing and related fields.

What does the Maths Curriculum at Aureus strive to achieve?
Our Mathematics curriculum builds a strong foundation for understanding the world, developing the ability to think and reason with confidence. We aim to nurture an appreciation of the patterns and importance of mathematics while fostering curiosity, enjoyment, and a willingness to explore new ideas.
How do students study Maths at Aureus?
Students learn Mathematics through a mastery approach that emphasises deep understanding, secure foundations, and the confidence to apply knowledge in new contexts. Concepts are introduced in small, carefully sequenced steps, allowing students to build fluency, reason mathematically, and solve problems with increasing independence. This approach ensures that learning is both accessible and challenging, enabling every student to make meaningful progress. In Key Stage 3, we teach in mixed ability classes, reflecting our commitment to inclusion and high expectations for all learners. Lessons are structured so that every student can access core ideas while also being stretched through rich tasks, reasoning challenges, and opportunities for deeper exploration. This approach supports collaboration, encourages mathematical discussion, and helps students learn from one another’s strategies and perspectives. As students move into Key Stage 4, they continue to build on these strong foundations as they begin their GCSE Mathematics course. At this stage, lessons are organised into Higher and Foundation tiers, allowing teaching to be closely aligned with the depth, pace, and content required for each pathway. This structure ensures that all students receive the appropriate level of challenge and support to achieve their best possible outcome at GCSE. Beyond the classroom, students benefit from a wide range of extra curricular opportunities designed to broaden their mathematical experience and nurture enthusiasm for the subject. Our Axiom Maths programme offers enrichment sessions for students who want to extend their thinking through puzzles, investigations, and advanced problemâsolving. We also run trips and events such as maths challenge competitions, STEM visits, and realâworld applications workshops, helping students see the relevance, creativity, and excitement of mathematics in everyday life.
Why is studying Maths important?
Mathematics is essential for every student because it equips them with the skills needed to understand and navigate an increasingly complex world. It develops logical thinking, problem solving, and the ability to make informed decisions—skills that underpin success in everyday life, further study, and almost every career path. Maths helps students interpret data, manage finances, understand patterns, and engage confidently with technology and science. Beyond its practical value, studying mathematics nurtures creativity, resilience, and the satisfaction that comes from tackling challenges and discovering elegant solutions. It is a subject that empowers young people to think clearly, reason effectively, and approach the world with curiosity and confidence. Curriculum Overview

GCSE Business Curriculum Map
The Edexcel GCSE (9–1) Business course introduces students to the world of small businesses and the processes involved in starting and growing an enterprise. It develops commercially minded and enterprising learners by exploring how business ideas emerge, how entrepreneurs respond to customer needs, and how organisations make decisions in a dynamic environment.
Students study two key themes: Investigating Small Business and Building a Business, which cover areas such as marketing, operations, finance, human resources, and external influences. This structure helps learners build from foundational concepts to a deeper understanding of how larger, established businesses operate and adapt. Throughout the course, students apply their knowledge to real-world examples, developing analytical, evaluative, and quantitative skills. By the end of the qualification, they gain a strong understanding of the business world and the ability to make informed judgments about business activity.
Year 10 Curriculum Overview - Business Studies
Year 10 typically covers the full Theme 1 content:Theme 1 focuses on how small businesses are established, identifying opportunities, and understanding the decisions entrepreneurs make when starting and running a business. It explores customer needs, market research, competition, business aims and objectives, financial planning, and the factors that influence the success of new enterprises. The theme builds foundational knowledge of enterprise, risk, reward, and the dynamic nature of business activity. Topics Covered in Year 10 (Theme 1)
1.1 Enterprise and Entrepreneurship Students learn what enterprise is, the role of entrepreneurs, and how new business ideas come about. 1.2 Spotting a Business Opportunity Focus on customer needs, market research, market segmentation, and understanding the competitive environment 1.3 Putting a Business Idea into Practice Introduction to aims and objectives, revenue, costs, profit, break-even, cash flow, and sources of finance. 1.4 Making the Business Effective Covers business location, the marketing mix, and producing business plans. 1.5 Understanding External Influences on Business Students explore stakeholders, technology, legislation, the economy, and how these external factors affect business decisions.
Year 11 Curriculum Overview - Business Studies
Theme 2 focuses on how businesses grow and the decisions they make as they expand. Students explore the key functional areas—marketing, operations, finance, and human resources—while also considering how external factors such as the economy, legislation, and technology influence business choices. The theme builds on the foundations of Theme 1, requiring students to analyse business performance, evaluate strategic decisions, and understand how established businesses compete in the wider market. Topics Covered in Year 11 (Theme 2) 2.1 Growing the Business Internal and external growth, sources of finance, and how expansion affects business aims and structure. 2.2 Making Marketing Decisions Applying the full marketing mix (4Ps) to help larger businesses compete effectively. 2.3 Making Operational Decisions Production processes, efficiency, and quality management in growing organisations. 2.4 Making Financial Decisions Analysing financial data to assess profitability, liquidity, and overall business performance. 2.5 Making Human Resource Decisions Organisational structures, recruitment, training, and motivation to support business growth. KS3 (Years 7-9)
Introduction to Business In KS3, students are introduced to the fundamentals of business through engaging, accessible activities that build curiosity and confidence. They learn essential business keywords and concepts—such as enterprise, entrepreneurs, profit, customers, and marketing—which lay the groundwork for the more detailed content they will encounter at GCSE. Students also gain practical experience by working in small groups to design, create, and run their own miniâbusinesses. This handsâon approach helps them understand how business ideas develop, how products and services are shaped by customer needs, and how teamwork and problemâsolving play a key role in successful enterprise. The KS3 programme is designed to spark interest, develop early analytical skills, and provide a strong foundation for future study in Business.

Headteacher's Weekly Update
Our Key Stage 4 Geography students had a fantastic field trip to Swanage, where they investigated coastal landscapes and geographical processes first hand. Experiencing geography beyond the classroom is such an important part of learning, and our students represented the school brilliantly throughout the visit.
We were also incredibly proud of a group of Year 8 students who attended the Oxford University Kids' 6th Conference. They delivered outstanding speeches, demonstrating confidence, maturity and excellent public speaking skills. It was wonderful to see them challenge themselves and embrace this prestigious opportunity.
This week, Humanutopia visited us to begin training our HEROes in preparation for Summer School. Our older students continue to impress us with their leadership, responsibility and commitment to supporting others. They are exceptional role models for our younger pupils and will play a vital role in helping our new Year 7 students feel welcomed, confident and excited as they prepare to join our school community in September. We are incredibly fortunate to have such caring and dedicated student leaders.
On Wednesday, we celebrated the remarkable art of our students with a stunning exhibition of artwork. The creativity, imagination and skill on display were truly inspiring and reflected the hard work and dedication of students across the school.
The celebrations continued into the evening with our annual Celebration Evening. This is always one of the highlights of the year, providing us with an opportunity to recognise students who consistently embody our school values in everything they do. Their achievements, character and contributions to our community make us immensely proud.
During the evening, we were also delighted to announce our new Head Prefects following a rigorous selection and interview process. I would like to congratulate those appointed and I would also like to acknowledge every student who put themselves forward. The quality of applications and interviews was exceptional, and each student demonstrated courage, ambition and a genuine desire to serve our school community. I am incredibly proud of how much they have grown and developed.
Towards the end of the week, our Year 7 students enjoyed an exciting trip to LEGOLAND, where they explored the world of robotics and engineering through hands on learning experiences. It was a fantastic opportunity to develop problem-solving, teamwork and technological skills in a fun and engaging environment.
Finally, our Year 10 Silver Duke of Edinburgh's Award students set off on their expedition. This challenging experience will test their resilience, teamwork and determination, and we wish them every success as they complete this important stage of their DofE journey.
As this week demonstrates, our students continue to embrace every opportunity available to them, whether in the classroom, out in the field, on stage, through leadership roles or whilst taking on new challenges. Their enthusiasm, commitment and achievements make us immensely proud.
Thank you, as always, for your continued support.
Kirsty Rogers Headteacher

Headteacher's Weekly Update
We were incredibly proud to see a number of our Year 8 students attend their The Brilliant Club Scholars Programme Graduation this week. The Brilliant Club has supported our students to experience university-style learning, guided by PhD researchers and academics. Throughout the programme, students took part in challenging tutorials, developed their critical thinking skills and completed a final assignment which is assessed using university grading criteria. Our Year 8 graduates demonstrated exceptional commitment, resilience and academic curiosity throughout the programme, and we were delighted to celebrate their success at graduation. They should be tremendously proud of everything they have achieved.
This week we have also been extremely proud of our Year 9 and Year 10 Heroes, who have supported our Rising Year 7 cohort during their transition days. They have shown outstanding leadership through their compassion, encouragement and confidence, helping our new students to feel welcomed, supported and excited about joining our school community in September. Their maturity and kindness ensured that our rising Year 7s enjoyed two wonderful days and gained a real sense of belonging. They have been exceptional ambassadors for our school and we are immensely proud of them.
On Friday, we waved off our World Challenge team as they embarked on their expedition to Morocco. Over the coming days they will be working alongside a local community, contributing to meaningful projects while developing their own resilience, independence and global awareness. Experiences such as these provide young people with invaluable opportunities to broaden their horizons, learn about different cultures and make a positive difference to the lives of others. We wish them a safe, rewarding and unforgettable journey and look forward to hearing all about their experiences when they return.
Our Year 7 students have also enjoyed a fantastic team-building day, filled with activities designed to strengthen friendships, develop confidence and foster a sense of community. For some students, the adventure continues this evening as they remain on site for our much-anticipated school camp out. We hope they have a wonderful evening making memories with their peers and staff.
Finally, we were very disappointed to have to postpone Sports Day this week due to the weather. However, we are pleased to confirm that Sports Day will now take place on Thursday 16th July. We know how much students and staff look forward to this event each year, and we cannot wait to celebrate the enthusiasm, teamwork and sporting spirit of our school community. I am also aware that many members of staff have been preparing for the eagerly anticipated staff race for quite some time, and I know students will be looking forward to cheering them on!
Thank you, as always, for your continued support. Have a wonderful weekend.
Kirsty Rogers Headteacher

Headteacher's Welcome
I am immensely proud to be the Headteacher of Aureus School. I have a passion for comprehensive education and I firmly believe that every student deserves the opportunity to succeed. My approach is driven by my belief in inclusive education and centred around high expectations of all students.
At Aureus School, we have been on a transformative journey and I am proud to share that this has resulted in a school where our students have a strong sense of belonging. We have an unwavering commitment to providing the best possible education for every student. We understand the importance of continuous growth and development, and we are dedicated to creating an environment where our students can thrive academically, socially, and emotionally.
As the only co-educational comprehensive school in Didcot we have a fantastic student body whose range of attributes contribute to making Aureus School a vibrant community. I have the privilege to be working with a dedicated and enthusiastic staff body who are passionate about inspiring our young people every single day, enabling them to thrive. As a community we believe in creating a learning environment that is both engaging and exciting, with an education that challenges our students to think critically and push boundaries. There is no limit to what our students can achieve and we provide the necessary support and resources so that everyone can succeed.
Our commitment to high expectations extends to behaviour as well. We believe that a stable and calm environment is essential for effective learning. Our personal development curriculum encourages kindness, acceptance, and an understanding of others’ views and opinions, fostering a sense of belonging and respect among our students. Our core values; Ambition, Resilience and Respect are threaded through everything that we do and we are proud of our students for showing these values everyday.
We offer a broad and balanced curriculum where students can thrive. We have an extensive selection of trips and visits, including Duke of Edinburgh expeditions, theatre productions, sporting events and trips abroad. Our school is always filled with the energy of sporting activities, STEM challenges and competitions, as well as music and drama performances and other artistic pursuits. The fantastic artwork our students produce can also be seen through handmade costumes, the amazing makeup in productions and also by simply walking around the school. At Aureus our extra-curricular opportunities combine to create a caring and highly successful school, where opportunities and experiences are highly valued.
As a parent I know that every family wants the very best for their young people; at Aureus we do too. Kirsty Rogers Headteacher
